en: “Incorrigible Chürök, you will never mend;
Since time beyond remembering,
You have never curbed your daring.
I would put an end to this,
Were you not moonlike Chürök,
And I would kill your slave!”
His heart was torn apart,
And tears poured from his eyes;
Taken captive and disgraced,
He longed desperately
To see the afflicted Choro just once.
Serving as a bondmaid,
Passing his days in slavery,
His hands secured and bound,
He suffered humiliation and lamented;
His senses failed and all turned dark,
And his days became unbearable torment.
Kyyaz thundered in his might,
While wretched Külchoro was humiliated;
He had fallen into an iron cage
And endured a sea of misery.
Brave Kyyaz of the Jediger
Had become a deep-dug pit for him;
Grieving, unable to find a way out,
Külchoro remained there,
Deprived of all six faculties.
Once Choro had been mighty,
But such was this calamitous horror
That might gave way to his disgrace.
Though he said, “Let me die,” he could not;
He could not take his own life.
He lived his days in slavery
And drank the bitter water of anguish;
His strength failed and left him helpless,
His former thunderous fury gone,
And he remained staring in supplication.
Had that Choro not come,
The true order would never have returned.
The destined hour had come:
Implacable death had reached Külchoro,
And it was time for him to die.
Choro’s beauty had faded;
His eyes stared wildly,
His legs hung limp,
And his living soul cried out.
His abundant, jewel-bright courage
Had wholly shattered and fled;
His vigor was spent and his strength gone.
Against Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
He had no deed left to attempt;
He scarcely seemed alive.
Choro, champion of the world,
Had no strength to act against Kyyaz.
Once Külchoro
Had been a lion favored by fortune,
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
Powerfully built and fierce of face—
Such a warrior he had been.
Now he yellowed with wasting sickness;
His destined hour had come.
After enduring countless torments,
It was time for Külchoro to die.
His black-collared felt coat
Had come apart layer by layer,
And lice spilled from its collar.
The torment of accursed humiliation
Was plainly visible there.
As for moonlike Aichürök,
That tumultuous woman of a thousand devices,
That headstrong woman—
How could we know what scheme
The nimble-witted infidel might devise?
In a prominent place stood a white palace,
Formidable in its strength;
A vast, resounding palace,
Immeasurable in its size.
It was encircled by ramparts,
Its gates were made of iron,
Its pillars were finely hewn,
And all around the cavernous building
Was brightly painted.
Its strength was plain for anyone to see;
Across its roof, side by side,
Three carts could have passed.
Into that towering palace
Chürök deliberately brought Choro.
Once he had entered the palace,
She sealed its entrance fast
And took Choro under her protection.
Sunlike Aichürök,
With her old maid who knew many things,
The noble-born heroine,
Her moonlike face gleaming,
Sixty buttons and forty keys
Jingling at her skirts—
Had you seen your sister-in-law Aichürök,
Her face shone like the sun
And swayed supple as fine leather.
Seeing Choro, she cried aloud;
The full-figured, luckless woman
Sobbed and wailed convulsively.
It seemed her ribs were breaking,
And tears streamed from her eyes;
She cried out and beat herself.
Burning with grief, Aichürök
Pleaded with Külchoro:
“You were our protector, our lion;
When this head was taken captive,
You alone were our guardian.
Though in anguish I said, ‘Let me die,’
The reason I remained alive
Was that you, my son, still lived.
Though in anguish I said, ‘Let me depart,’
The reason I stayed alive and safe
When Kyyaz took me captive,
When he heaped torment upon my head,
When my plight became dire
And he gashed my side—
Your sunlike sister-in-law Aichürök,
Bound as though guilty,
Lamenting with no escape,
Her head trapped in a narrow gorge,
Her precious self disgraced,
Wandered out this way,
Delirious as though possessed.
From the one Creator, Almighty God,
It was you I prayed for.
So I refrained from spilling my blood
And could not bring myself to end my life.
I did not kill myself,
My valiant, cherished son,
And today I have seen your face.
You were terribly late in coming;
Today I entrust to you
The sole survivor left in our need.
The foal left by the great stallion,
I reared until he grew—
The young hawk left by the falcon.
Take your ill-fated younger brother
As your companion,
And spread terror among the foe!
Destroy all sorrow;
My son, become your former self!
With broad ornaments and ample hips,
I was once your stately sister-in-law,
Who drove white deer and tamed them like cattle,
Who subdued the whole wide world,
Who confounded everyone she met,
Broke roads through narrow places,
And attacked many lands.
You were the peerless eagle.
When we remember your elder brother,
We mourn and wail without end,
Yet pray in hope, saying, ‘Choro remains in his place.’
We live on, offering our prayers.
You were the Morning Star of the people,
And I was the mother of the nation!
While you lived, my son,
We burned and blazed with longing.
Wondering, ‘When will my son return?’
I, black-faced Aichürök,
Lived yearning for you.
You shattered hills and opened roads;
You broke into Beijing and attacked.
You shattered stone and opened roads;
You assailed the whole wide world.
You were a lion of exalted spirit;
While my son Choro lived,
I used to say, ‘What calamity could touch us?’
None who fled you escaped alive;
You were a blue-maned panther.
I was your wailing sister-in-law,
A royal treasure, wealth that never diminishes.
May this false world come to an end!
You overthrew Afghanistan to its roots;
What ancient nation remained unharmed?
You conquered Künjüt and Khotan
And attacked Hindustan.
No land remained whole
Where your stallion had not wheeled;
No nation remained whole
Where Külchoro had not thrust his spear.
You were both warrior and lion;
A vast river-lake
That could never be emptied by drawing;
A broad and noble valley
Whose grass could never be exhausted by grazing.
You were a gray-winged hunting bird
That let no bustard settle on the steppe;
A boundlessly sharp blade of steel
Destined to meet the warrior sultan.
You were a forest fortress in a sheltered bend,
Untouched by wind when storms arose;
You never bowed to an enemy,
But were a ravenous lion.
Saying, ‘When will the lion’s son return?’
I was the sister-in-law who prayed for you.
As Kyyaz’s captive,
I endured his cruelty for long.
You never left my thoughts, my son;
I lived wondering when you would return.
It seems God has opened the door to my fortune:
The lost champion has been found,
The man I lacked has returned,
What departed has been restored,
My grief has been covered over—
It seems God has granted this before my eyes!
The one who vanished without a trace,
My blue-maned wolf of a son, seems to have returned.
I prayed for you with bitter cries.
Knowing that you had gone,
I took your elder brother’s bulletproof armor—
The precious thing, all of it together—
And put it in a great saddlebag.
I wrapped every piece together,
Thinking, ‘When my son comes, let him wear it;
Let him strike the enemy without tiring;
Let him make merry havoc;
Let him lay Kyyaz of the Jediger
Full length upon the ground;
Let him avenge his unavenged wrong;
Let him drag the Jediger of Jeti-Özön
Along the road
And make a spectacle of them before the Danggits.’
I have this precious marvel;
Listen, my fiery son:
I had a coat specially made—
Its back of iron, its sleeves of copper,
Its thickness half a cubit.
I proofed it against direct arrow shots;
It was intended for head-on battle,
And it greatly depleted the treasury.
Anything unfit was rejected with curses;
Steel was filed down and glued,
Then poured across every part.
With awls made of steel,
Immeasurably mighty champions
Stitched it with pounding blows;
When struck with a spear,
The spearhead bent and flew aside.
When battling an enemy,
When fighting face-to-face,
They wondered, ‘Could an arrow pierce it?’
And said, ‘It would be folly not to find out.’
Alas, it was seized from me;
When Kyyaz took my precious,
Costly bulletproof armor,
Alas, I had it torn apart.
I brought what remained in trust,
Thinking, ‘Let my sorrow-dispelling son wear it.’
I give it to you as a gift—wear it and prosper!
Arm yourself and strike the foe!
My cherished son, wear
The bulletproof armor I had specially made,
And charge to attack the enemy!
Strike the Jediger of Jeti-Özön
